section.title: The Ten Commandments
section.sectionRationale: This is the heart of the Sinai covenant, the ten words spoken directly by God to the whole nation, still trembling from the mountain's fire. They summarize the whole moral shape of a life rightly ordered toward God and neighbor, and the people's terror at hearing God's own voice shows why a mediator is needed.
section.thesis: Having identified Himself as the God who redeemed Israel from slavery, the LORD speaks ten commandments covering love for Him alone and love for neighbor; the people, terrified by His voice, ask Moses to mediate, and Moses explains that this fear is meant to keep them from sin.
section.frameNote: Seven movements: the LORD's self-identification and the first command, no other gods; the prohibition of idols; the command against misusing God's name; the Sabbath command; honoring parents; the five commands concerning neighbor, life, marriage, property, truth, and desire; and the people's terrified request for a mediator.

units.label: I am the LORD your God

media.alt: A mountain wrapped in smoke and fire
media.caption: God speaks all these words from the fire of Sinai.

verses.text: And God spoke all these words:
“I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.
You shall have no other gods before Me.

units.label: No idols
units.note: a jealous God, loving devotion to a thousand generations

verses.text: You shall not make for yourself an {{idol|idol}} in the form of anything in the heavens above, on the earth below, or in the waters beneath.

You shall not bow down to them or worship them; for I, the LORD your God, am a {{jealous|jealous}} God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers on their children to the third and fourth generations of those who hate Me,
but showing loving devotion to a thousand generations of those who love Me and keep My commandments.
You shall not take the {{name|name}} of the LORD your God in vain, for the LORD will not leave anyone unpunished who takes His name in vain.
{{remember|Remember}} the Sabbath day by keeping it holy.
Six days you shall labor and do all your work,

but the seventh day is a Sabbath to the LORD your God, on which you must not do any work, neither you, nor your son or daughter, nor your manservant or maidservant or livestock, nor the foreigner within your gates.
For in six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth and the sea and all that is in them, but on the seventh day He rested. Therefore the LORD blessed the Sabbath day and set it apart as holy.

units.label: Honor father and mother
units.note: so that your days may be long

verses.text: Honor your father and mother, so that your days may be long in the land that the LORD your God is giving you.
You shall not murder.
You shall not commit adultery.
You shall not steal.
You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor.
You shall not covet your neighbor's house. You shall not covet your neighbor's wife, or his manservant or maidservant, or his ox or donkey, or anything that belongs to your neighbor.”

units.label: The people's fear, and a mediator
units.note: let God not speak to us, or we will die

verses.text: When all the people witnessed the thunder and lightning, the sounding of the ram's horn, and the mountain enveloped in smoke, they trembled and stood at a distance.
“Speak to us yourself and we will listen,” they said to Moses. “But do not let God speak to us, or we will die.”
“Do not be afraid,” Moses replied. “For God has come to test you, so that the fear of Him may be before you, to keep you from sinning.”
And the people stood at a distance as Moses approached the thick darkness where God was.

idol.gloss: A carved image, an idol shaped by human hands. The command forbids not only worshiping other gods but manufacturing any physical representation to worship, since no image can capture the living God who speaks and acts.

jealous.gloss: Jealous, zealous, allowing no rival. Applied to God, this is not petty insecurity but the fierce, faithful exclusivity appropriate to a covenant relationship, the same word used of a husband's rightful claim on his wife's fidelity.

name.gloss: Emptiness, falsehood, vanity, worthlessness. To take God's name shav is to invoke it carelessly, falsely, or for empty purposes, whether in false oaths, careless speech, or claiming His authority for what He has not said.

remember.gloss: Remember, an active, ongoing recollection meant to shape behavior, not a passing thought. Israel is to zakhor the Sabbath continually, letting the memory of God's own creation rest reorder their entire working week.

basic.context: God speaks these ten commands directly to the whole nation of Israel from the fire and smoke of Sinai, right after they have promised to obey. They cover how to love God rightly and how to love neighbor rightly, and the people are so terrified by hearing God's own voice that they beg Moses to speak for them instead.
basic.hermeneutics: These are real, historical words spoken to a real covenant nation. Christians are not bound to keep every Old Testament ceremonial or civil law tied to Israel's specific nationhood, but the moral core of the Ten Commandments reflects God's unchanging character and is renewed, not abolished, in the New Testament's call to love God and neighbor.
basic.originalLanguages: God forbids any pesel, carved image, to represent Him, because He is qanna, jealous, rightly allowing no rival. To take His name shav, in vain or emptiness, is to misuse His authority. And Israel must zakhor, actively remember, the Sabbath, letting God's own creation rest shape their whole rhythm of work and rest.
basic.typology: The whole law given here, meant to be perfectly kept, exposes humanity's need for someone who actually keeps it; Jesus is that someone, fulfilling the law completely, Matthew 5:17, so that His righteousness, not our imperfect obedience, becomes the ground of our standing before God.
basic.christ: Jesus summarizes these ten commands as love for God and love for neighbor, Matthew 22:37-40, and He alone perfectly kept every one of them on behalf of His people. Where Israel trembled before the law's demand, believers now approach God through Christ, who fulfilled the law and bore its curse, Galatians 3:13.
basic.god: God is holy enough that His own people cannot bear to hear His voice directly, and He is also the one who redeemed them before ever giving a single command, 'I am the LORD your God, who brought you out.' Grace precedes law here; the commandments describe the shape of a life already rescued, not a ladder to climb toward rescue.
basic.crossReferences: Matthew 22:37-40 summarizes the whole law as love for God and neighbor. Romans 13:8-10 shows love fulfilling the specific commands about neighbor. Galatians 3:13 says Christ redeemed us from the law's curse by becoming a curse for us. Hebrews 12:18-21 recalls the people's terror at Sinai.
basic.oneStory: God rescues His people first, then gives them commands that describe how a rescued people are to live, loving Him wholly and their neighbor genuinely. The law's demand, impossible to keep perfectly, drives the whole story toward Christ, who keeps it fully and gives His righteousness to everyone who trusts Him.

context.literary:
Scripture never calls these 'the Ten Commandments' in the Hebrew; it calls them 'the ten words,' Exodus 34:28, Deuteronomy 4:13 and 10:4, which is where the name Decalogue comes from. Exodus 20:1 introduces them simply: 'God spoke all these words.' Everything that follows in chapters 21 to 23 is introduced differently, as 'the ordinances' Moses is to set before the people, Exodus 21:1. The ten words stand apart as the only part of the law the whole nation heard directly from God.

The ten words begin not with a command but with a self-introduction and a history: 'I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery,' verse 2. That prologue governs everything after it. The commands are the terms of a relationship that already exists.

The form is strikingly uneven. Some words are a few Hebrew words long; the three commands of verses 13 to 15 are just two words each in Hebrew, a negative and a verb. Others are expanded with reasons and motives. The command against images carries a warning and a promise, verses 5 and 6; the name command a threat, verse 7; the Sabbath a full explanation rooted in creation, verses 8 to 11; the command to honour parents a promise of long life, verse 12. The fuller commands are those where Israel was most likely to go wrong or to need persuading.

The sequence moves from God to neighbour, and within the neighbour commands from the most visible acts to the most hidden: life, marriage, property, testimony, and finally desire. The last command reaches into the heart, where no human court could follow.

The narrative frame matters as much as the list. Chapter 19 ended with Moses going down to the people, and chapter 20 closes with the people standing at a distance while Moses draws near 'the thick darkness where God was,' verse 21. The ten words are spoken between two scenes of fear, and the second scene explains why a mediator will carry the rest of the law.
context.historical:
The covenant form of this passage resembles the treaties of the ancient Near East, in which a great king identified himself, recalled what he had done for his vassal, and then set out the vassal's obligations. Many scholars have pointed to Hittite treaties of the second millennium as especially close parallels, with their historical prologues, stipulations, and provisions for depositing the text. Israel's covenant has these features: the LORD names Himself, recalls the exodus, and gives His terms, and the tablets are later placed in the ark, the covenant's sacred depository. The difference is decisive. No other people had a god who bound them to himself by covenant in this way, and the first stipulation is exclusive loyalty to Him alone.

The tablets were 'inscribed by the finger of God,' Exodus 31:18, and 'inscribed on both sides, front and back,' Exodus 32:15. The traditional picture of two tablets with four or five commands on each is not stated in the text. It may be that each tablet carried the whole text, as treaty copies were given to both parties, though this too is a proposal rather than a certainty.

The commands fit the life of a people about to settle a land. The household in verse 10 includes sons and daughters, male and female servants, livestock and 'the foreigner within your gates.' The Sabbath was a gift even to the lowest members of the household. Deuteronomy's version makes that explicit: 'so that your manservant and maidservant may rest as you do,' Deuteronomy 5:14. In the ancient world, a day of rest for slaves and animals was unusual.

The prohibition of images stood against the entire religious culture of Egypt and Canaan, where the gods were worshipped through statues believed to host divine presence. The command against coveting names the household goods of a farming family: house, wife, servants, ox and donkey. The law addresses ordinary life, not an idealised world.
context.canonical:
The ten words are repeated in Deuteronomy 5:6-21, where Moses recites them to the new generation. The differences are instructive. The Sabbath command begins with 'Observe' rather than 'Remember,' and its reason is the exodus rather than creation: 'Remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt,' Deuteronomy 5:15. The coveting command places the wife first and adds 'field,' Deuteronomy 5:21. Deuteronomy also records God's response to the people's fear: 'They have done well in all that they have spoken. If only they had such a heart to fear Me,' Deuteronomy 5:28-29, and it is from this request at Horeb that the promise of a prophet like Moses arises, Deuteronomy 18:15-17.

The prophets use the commands as the charge sheet against Israel. Jeremiah asks, 'Will you steal and murder, commit adultery and perjury, burn incense to Baal, and follow other gods?' Jeremiah 7:9. Hosea lists 'cursing and lying, murder and stealing, and adultery,' Hosea 4:2. Both then look forward to a covenant in which God will write the law on the heart, Jeremiah 31:33, and give a new heart and His Spirit, Ezekiel 36:26-27.

The New Testament quotes the ten words often, as the BSB footnotes on verses 12 to 17 record. Jesus lists several of them for the rich young man, Matthew 19:18-19, and deepens murder and adultery to anger and lust, Matthew 5:21-28. Paul says he would not have known coveting if the law had not said 'Do not covet,' Romans 7:7, and that the neighbour commands 'are summed up' in 'Love your neighbor as yourself,' Romans 13:9. James argues that the one who said 'Do not commit adultery' also said 'Do not murder,' James 2:11, and Ephesians 6:2-3 calls the parents' command 'the first commandment with a promise.' Hebrews 12:18-21 recalls the scene of verses 18 and 19 to show the difference between Sinai and Zion.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses wanted Israel to know first who was speaking. The God who gives these words is the same God who broke their chains. Obedience was to flow from gratitude and loyalty, not from fear of a stranger. That is why the first word is not a demand but a name and a history.

He also wanted Israel to see that life with God and life with neighbour are one fabric. The same voice forbids other gods and forbids theft. Worship that tolerates injustice is not the worship this God accepts, as the prophets would later insist, Jeremiah 7:9-10. And the order teaches that right relationship with God is the root from which right relationship with neighbour grows.

The address is in the singular throughout, 'you shall not,' as though God were speaking to each Israelite personally. The covenant is national, but obedience is personal. No one could hide in the crowd.

Finally, Moses wanted Israel to understand the purpose of the fear they felt. 'God has come to test you, so that the fear of Him may be before you, to keep you from sinning,' verse 20. The terror of the mountain was not meant to drive them away from God but to root a lasting reverence in them. Those who fear Him rightly do not need to be afraid of Him in the wrong way.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Unlike much Old Testament narrative, this passage is prescription in the fullest sense: God commands. The question is how commands given to Israel apply to believers now. The New Testament answers by reaffirming nine of the ten words as still binding on Christians, quoting several of them directly, often deepened by Jesus, Matthew 5:21-28, and summed up in love, Romans 13:9. Idolatry, profanity, dishonour of parents, murder, adultery, theft, lies and coveting remain sin.

The Sabbath is the one command the New Testament treats differently. Jesus calls Himself 'Lord even of the Sabbath,' Mark 2:28, and Paul lists the Sabbath among things that are 'a shadow of the things to come, but the body that casts it belongs to Christ,' Colossians 2:16-17. Christians have understood this in different ways, from keeping the Lord's Day as a Christian Sabbath to seeing the command fulfilled in the rest Christ gives, Hebrews 4:9-10. Almost all agree that the rhythm of work and rest, and the dedication of time to God, still reflect His design.

What the passage also describes is the people's fear and their request for a mediator. That is recorded rather than commanded, but God approves it, Deuteronomy 5:28, and it points beyond Moses to Christ.

debates.question: Is it right to divide the law given at Sinai into moral, civil, and ceremonial categories?

views.label: The traditional threefold division
views.case: Many theologians, especially in the Reformed tradition, distinguish the ten words as enduring moral law, the case laws of chapters 21 to 23 as civil law for Israel's nationhood, and the tabernacle and sacrificial instructions as ceremonial law fulfilled in Christ. The unique status of the ten words, spoken by God's own voice and written by His finger, supports treating them as a summary of moral law.

views.label: Caution about the division's limits
views.case: Others note that Scripture does not explicitly categorise the law this way, and that moral, civil and ceremonial elements are interwoven even within the ten words, as the Sabbath's ties to both creation and Israel's covenant sign show, Exodus 31:13. They prefer to read the whole law as fulfilled in Christ and to learn its abiding moral shape from the way the New Testament itself uses it.

debates.bearing: Both views agree that the moral substance of the ten words, love for God and neighbour, remains binding, while the specific national and ceremonial forms given to Israel are fulfilled in Christ. The debate concerns how neatly the lines can be drawn, not whether the law's moral heart still matters.

debates.question: How should the ten words be numbered?

views.label: The Jewish division
views.case: In Jewish tradition verse 2, 'I am the LORD your God, who brought you out,' is the first word, and verses 3 to 6, no other gods and no images, form the second. The text itself calls them 'words' rather than commands, so a declaration can count as one. This keeps the redemption at the head of the list.

views.label: The Catholic and Lutheran division
views.case: Following Augustine, these traditions treat verses 3 to 6 as a single command against false worship and divide verse 17 into two, coveting a neighbour's house and coveting his wife. Support comes from Deuteronomy 5:21, which separates the wife from the house and uses a different verb for each.

views.label: The Reformed and Orthodox division
views.case: This numbering, found in ancient writers such as Philo and Josephus and in much of the early church, treats no other gods and no images as two commands and verse 17 as one. It notes that worshipping another god and worshipping the true God through an image are different sins, as the golden calf would show, Exodus 32:4-5.

debates.bearing: The text says there are ten and does not number them, so certainty is not possible. The substance is the same in every system. The differences matter most for the image command, which the Reformed numbering highlights, reminding Christians that the true God may be worshipped wrongly as well as false gods worshipped.

study.originalLanguages:
The opening self-declaration uses anokhi, the fuller form of 'I,' and the singular 'your God.' Throughout the ten words Israel is addressed as 'you' singular. In English the plural and singular 'you' look the same, but in Hebrew the whole nation is addressed as though it were one person, and each Israelite would hear the words as spoken to himself or herself. The phrase 'house of slavery,' beit avadim, recalls Exodus 13:3 and returns in Deuteronomy 5:6. Egypt was not only a place but a household in which Israel had been owned.

Most of the commands use the negative lo with the imperfect verb. Hebrew has a milder way of saying 'do not,' used for immediate situations; this construction states a permanent, categorical prohibition. It is the form of law that admits no exceptions for circumstance. Verse 3's 'before Me' is literally 'upon My face' or 'in My presence,' and the BSB footnote gives 'besides Me.' Either way, no rival is to stand where God can see it, and there is nowhere He cannot see.

Verse 6 promises 'loving devotion,' chesed, to 'a thousand generations,' and the footnote notes it may be 'to thousands.' The contrast is still stark. Punishment reaches to the third and fourth generation 'of those who hate Me,' that is, a household that continues in the fathers' hatred, while mercy reaches to thousands. The same proportion reappears in God's self-description in Exodus 34:6-7, and Deuteronomy 24:16 and Ezekiel 18:20 make clear that no child is punished for a parent's sin in which he has no share.

The third command literally forbids 'lifting up' or 'carrying,' nasa, the name. It is the verb used when Aaron is to 'bear' Israel's names on his shoulders before God, Exodus 28:12. Israel carried the LORD's name as His people; the command forbids bearing it emptily, whether in false oaths, careless speech or a life that contradicts it. Deuteronomy's ninth command uses the same word for emptiness, 'witness of shav,' where Exodus 20:16 has 'witness of sheqer,' falsehood, Deuteronomy 5:20.

'Honor,' kabbed, comes from the root meaning heavy or weighty, the root of kavod, glory. To honour parents is to give them weight, to treat them as significant. The same verb is used of honouring God, 'Honor the LORD with your wealth,' Proverbs 3:9.

'You shall not murder' uses ratsach. It is not the general word for killing, and it is not the word normally used for killing in battle. It belongs to the language of the laws on manslaughter and murder, and it is even used for the one who kills 'unintentionally' in Numbers 35:11. Its range is the personal taking of a human life that the community must answer for, and the command forbids the unlawful taking of life.

The last command uses chamad, to desire or covet. It is the word for the tree that was 'desirable' in Genesis 3:6 and for Achan's confession, 'I coveted them and took them,' Joshua 7:21. The law ends where the first sin began, with a desire that reaches for what God has not given.

Finally, in verse 20 Moses says God has come 'to test' them, nissah, the verb of Massah, Exodus 17:7, and of God testing Abraham, Genesis 22:1. He plays on fear: 'Do not be afraid,' yet 'the fear of Him' should remain before them. Moses then approaches 'the thick darkness,' araphel, the dark cloud in which, Solomon later says, the LORD dwells, 1 Kings 8:12.

typology.type: The law written on tablets of stone
typology.fulfillment: The ten words were written by God's finger on stone, Exodus 31:18, a permanent text outside the people. Jeremiah promised that God would one day 'inscribe it on their hearts,' Jeremiah 31:33, and Paul says believers are 'a letter from Christ... written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts,' 2 Corinthians 3:3. The escalation is from an external standard to an inward disposition worked by the Spirit, Romans 8:4. The type does not fall away: the same law is now written within. What changes is where it is written and who gives the power to keep it.

typology.type: Moses approaching the thick darkness for a trembling people
typology.fulfillment: The people ask Moses to speak to them in God's place, and he alone draws near to the dark cloud, verses 19 and 21. God approves the request and promises 'a prophet like me,' Deuteronomy 18:15-18. Christ is that prophet and more. He does not merely enter the darkness and return; He comes from the Father's side and 'has made Him known,' John 1:18. Hebrews contrasts the Sinai scene, where even Moses said 'I am trembling with fear,' Hebrews 12:21, with the approach believers now have to 'Jesus the mediator of a new covenant,' Hebrews 12:24. Moses shielded the people from God's voice; Christ brings them to hear it without terror.

typology.type: The Sabbath rest after six days of work
typology.fulfillment: The Sabbath command roots Israel's week in God's rest after creation, verse 11, and Deuteronomy adds the rest of freedom from slavery, Deuteronomy 5:15. Hebrews reads the Sabbath as pointing beyond itself: 'There remains, then, a Sabbath rest for the people of God,' and whoever enters God's rest 'also rests from his own work,' Hebrews 4:9-10. Jesus calls Himself 'Lord even of the Sabbath,' Mark 2:28, and invites the weary to find rest in Him, Matthew 11:28. The weekly day was a shadow; the body that casts it 'belongs to Christ,' Colossians 2:17. The type falls short because one day in seven could only interrupt labour, while Christ gives rest to the soul.

typology.type: The redeemer who speaks before He commands
typology.fulfillment: The ten words begin with 'I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery,' verse 2. Redemption comes first, then obligation. The New Testament keeps exactly that order in Christ. 'God sent His Son, born of a woman, born under the law, to redeem those under the law,' Galatians 4:4-5, and only then comes the call to live as sons. Jesus says, 'If you love Me, you will keep My commandments,' John 14:15. The escalation is from rescue out of Egypt to redemption from sin and the curse of the law, Galatians 3:13.

study.christ:
The ten words lead to Christ first by the order in which they are given. Before a single command, God names Himself as redeemer. The gospel follows the same order: Christ redeems, and then He calls His people to obey. He was 'born under the law, to redeem those under the law,' Galatians 4:4-5. The commands are not the ladder to God; they are the shape of the life He gives to those He has already brought out.

They lead to Christ by His own fulfilment of them. Jesus lived under these words as an Israelite and kept them without failure. He could ask, 'Which of you can prove Me guilty of sin?' John 8:46, and Hebrews says He was 'tempted in every way that we are, yet was without sin,' Hebrews 4:15. He did not only avoid murder and adultery; He kept the commands at the depth He Himself taught, where anger and lust are measured, Matthew 5:21-28. He had no other god before His Father, honoured His mother even from the cross, John 19:26-27, and never coveted, for He 'emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant,' Philippians 2:7. His obedience is the righteousness credited to those who believe. 'Christ is the end of the law, to bring righteousness to everyone who believes,' Romans 10:4.

They lead to Christ by exposing the need for Him. Paul says that the commandment 'Do not covet' made him aware of sin, Romans 7:7. The law is 'holy, righteous, and good,' Romans 7:12, and exactly for that reason it reveals how far every human heart falls short. 'The law became our guardian to lead us to Christ, that we might be justified by faith,' Galatians 3:24.

They lead to Christ by the mediator scene at the end of the passage. The people cannot bear God's voice and ask for someone to stand between. God approves the request and promises the prophet like Moses, Deuteronomy 18:15-17. The transfiguration names Him: 'This is My beloved Son... Listen to Him!' Matthew 17:5. In Christ God speaks without the thunder that drove Israel back, and 'the one and only Son... has made Him known,' John 1:18.

They lead to Christ by the promise of a new heart. What the tablets of stone could command, the Spirit of Christ writes within. God sent His Son 'so that the righteous standard of the law might be fulfilled in us, who do not walk according to the flesh but according to the Spirit,' Romans 8:4. Jesus reduces the commands not to a vague feeling but to love, 'All the Law and the Prophets hang on these two commandments,' Matthew 22:40, and He shows what that love looks like by laying down His life.

A caution is in order. Not every command is a coded picture of Christ, and the passage is first of all law for Israel. Its link to Christ runs through His keeping of it, His fulfilment of it, and His giving of the Spirit, not through allegory.
study.god:
The first thing the ten words show about God is that He introduces Himself. 'I am the LORD your God,' verse 2. He is not an unknown force to be guessed at but a person with a name, a history and a people. The God of Sinai reveals Himself by word, and the commands are an unveiling of His character as much as a list of duties.

He is one and exclusive. 'You shall have no other gods before Me,' verse 3. This is not the demand of an insecure deity but the claim of the only God there is. His jealousy, verse 5, is the jealousy of a husband for a wife, not the envy of a rival. Exodus 34:14 goes so far as to say His name is Jealous. Love that did not care whether its beloved went after others would not be love.

He is spirit and cannot be imaged. The prohibition of images follows from the fact that Israel 'saw no form' at Sinai, Deuteronomy 4:12. Any image would shrink Him to the size of a creature. The only image of God Scripture approves is the human person, and ultimately the Son, who is 'the image of the invisible God,' Colossians 1:15.

He is both just and abundantly merciful. The punishment of verse 5 is real, but the mercy of verse 6 is to a thousand generations. God's anger is measured; His loving devotion overflows. The disproportion is deliberate and becomes the backbone of Israel's confession in Exodus 34:6-7.

He is the Creator and the one who rests. The Sabbath command grounds Israel's week in God's own pattern, 'in six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth... but on the seventh day He rested,' verse 11. God is not a restless deity who needs human labour to sustain Him. He works and then rests in the goodness of His work, and He invites His people, including servants, foreigners and animals, into that rest. His rest is generous.

He cares about the whole of human life. The same God who forbids idolatry forbids theft and lying, protects marriage and life and honours parents. His holiness is not detached from ordinary relationships; it is expressed in them. And He looks at the heart: the last command forbids a desire that no one else can see.

He is holy and frightening, and yet His purpose in the fear is kind. 'God has come to test you, so that the fear of Him may be before you, to keep you from sinning,' verse 20. He does not terrify to destroy but to protect. The God who dwells in thick darkness, verse 21, is the same God who wants His people to live.

For worship, the ten words teach that God is to be loved with an undivided heart, approached as He has revealed Himself and not as we imagine Him, named with reverence, trusted with our time, and honoured in how we treat every neighbour.

crossReferences.note: The second giving of the ten words to the next generation. The Sabbath is grounded in redemption rather than creation, 'Remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt,' verse 15, and the coveting command separates the wife from the house. Together the two versions show creation and redemption as twin foundations of Israel's rest.

Moses' account of the people's request for a mediator adds God's own response: 'They have done well in all that they have spoken. If only they had such a heart to fear Me.' God approves the fear of Exodus 20:18-20 and longs for the inward heart that only the new covenant will supply.

The promise of 'a prophet like me' arises directly from this scene: 'This is what you asked of the LORD your God at Horeb.' The people's plea in Exodus 20:19 becomes the seed of the hope for a greater mediator, fulfilled in Christ, Acts 3:22.

Jeremiah's temple sermon reads like the Decalogue in reverse: steal, murder, commit adultery, perjury, and follow other gods, then come to the temple and say 'We are delivered.' The prophet uses the ten words to expose worship that has been detached from obedience.

The new covenant promise answers the tablets of stone. God will 'put My law in their minds and inscribe it on their hearts.' The law does not change; its location does. What was written by God's finger on stone at Sinai will be written by His Spirit within His people, as Hebrews 8:10 confirms.

Jesus quotes 'Do not murder' and 'Do not commit adultery' and deepens both to anger and lustful looking. He does not replace the ten words but shows how far they reach, into the heart that the tenth command already addressed. The law's claim is total, and only Christ has fully met it.

Paul says he would not have known coveting if the law had not said 'Do not covet.' The command of Exodus 20:17 exposed desire he could not master, and yet 'the law is holy, and the commandment is holy, righteous, and good.' The fault lies with sin, not with God's word.

Paul quotes four of the neighbour commands and says they are 'summed up in this one decree: Love your neighbor as yourself.' Love does not abolish the commands; it fulfils them. The ten words describe what love refuses to do, and love supplies the motive the list itself cannot give.

James argues that the law is a unity because it comes from one Lawgiver: 'He who said, Do not commit adultery, also said, Do not murder.' Breaking any one command is breaking faith with the God who spoke all of them, the point of Exodus 20:1, 'God spoke all these words.'

Paul calls 'Honor your father and mother' 'the first commandment with a promise' and applies the promise of Exodus 20:12 to children in the church. He widens 'in the land' to 'on the earth,' showing how a covenant blessing tied to Canaan is carried over to believers everywhere.

Believers are 'a letter from Christ... not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts.' Paul sets the Spirit's work against the stone tablets given at Sinai. The same holy standard is now written inwardly, so that obedience comes from a changed heart rather than external pressure.

Hebrews recalls the fire, darkness, trumpet and 'a voice that made its hearers beg that no further word be spoken,' the scene of Exodus 20:18-19. Believers have come instead to Mount Zion and to Jesus, the mediator whose blood speaks a better word. The God is the same; the access is new.

study.oneStory:
In the garden God gave one command and a world of freedom around it, and the first sin began with a desire for what He had withheld, Genesis 3:6. At Sinai God gives ten words to a redeemed people, and the last of them forbids that very desire. The ten words are a portrait of the life humanity was made for and lost: God loved without rivals, His name honoured, His rest enjoyed, parents honoured, life, marriage, property and truth protected, and the heart content with what God gives.

The passage answers the story so far. God promised Abraham a people, rescued that people from Egypt, and carried them to Himself. Now He tells them how to live as His people. The prologue, 'who brought you out,' connects the law to the exodus, and the Sabbath connects it to creation. Law is not a new plan; it is the shape of life under the Creator and Redeemer.

It also sets up what follows, and the story turns quickly. Before Moses has even come down from the mountain, Israel breaks the opening commands at the golden calf, Exodus 32, and Moses shatters the tablets. The rest of the Old Testament shows the same pattern on a national scale, until the prophets charge Israel with breaking the ten words one by one, Jeremiah 7:9 and Hosea 4:2. The law reveals the holiness of God and the sin of His people, but it cannot change the heart. The people's fear at Sinai leaves them standing at a distance, verse 21.

The story comes to rest in Christ. He is the Israelite who kept every word, the prophet like Moses who speaks God's word without thunder, and the Redeemer who bore the law's curse, Galatians 3:13. Through Him the Spirit writes the law on His people's hearts, Jeremiah 31:33 and 2 Corinthians 3:3, and love becomes the fulfilment of the law, Romans 13:10.

In the new creation the ten words will not be abolished but fully realised. No idolaters, murderers, sexually immoral or lovers of falsehood will be inside the city, Revelation 22:15, not because the law will be enforced by fear but because God's people will be made like Christ. They will love God with all their heart and their neighbour as themselves. The Sabbath rest will be permanent, and the people who once stood far off will live in the presence of the God who spoke from the fire.

sermon.title: Who Takes First Place?
sermon.why: Part of Begg's 'Pathway to Freedom' series on the Ten Commandments, this sermon on Exodus 20:3 explains how the first commandment requires exclusive worship of God and exposes every rival that clamors for that place in the heart.

quiz.q: How does God introduce Himself before giving any of the Ten Commandments?

options.text: As the LORD their God, who brought them out of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.
options.note: Verse 2 shows grace and redemption stated before any command is given.

options.text: As a distant judge with no prior relationship to Israel.
options.note: God explicitly identifies Himself by His prior act of redemption, not distant impersonality.

options.text: As one god among many for Israel to consider.
options.note: The commandments that follow, especially verse 3, make clear He alone is to be worshiped, not one option among many.

options.text: No introduction is given before the commandments.
options.note: Verse 2 gives a clear, redemptive self-introduction before the first command.

quiz.q: What reason does God give for keeping the Sabbath, according to verse 11?

options.text: Because He made the heavens and earth in six days and rested on the seventh.
options.note: The command is explicitly rooted in the pattern of creation itself.

options.text: Because Pharaoh had forced Israel to work seven days a week.
options.note: While rest matters after slavery, this verse specifically grounds the command in creation, not merely relief from Egypt.

options.text: Because the seventh day was considered unlucky.
options.note: No such superstition is given; the reasoning is theological, rooted in creation.

options.text: No reason is given for the Sabbath command.
options.note: Verse 11 explicitly grounds it in God's own pattern of creation and rest.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the Ten Commandments given in this chapter?

options.text: You shall tithe a tenth of all your produce.
options.note: Tithing is commanded elsewhere in the law, but it is not one of the Ten Commandments listed here.

options.text: You shall not murder.
options.note: This is explicitly one of the ten, verse 13.

options.text: You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor.
options.note: This is explicitly one of the ten, verse 16.

options.text: You shall not covet your neighbor's house.
options.note: This is explicitly one of the ten, verse 17.

quiz.q: How did the people respond after witnessing the thunder, lightning, and smoke at the mountain?

options.text: They trembled, stood at a distance, and asked Moses to speak to them instead of God directly.
options.note: Verses 18 to 19 record this terrified request for a mediator.

options.text: They rushed forward eagerly to touch the mountain themselves.
options.note: The opposite occurred; they stood at a distance in fear, not eagerness to approach.

options.text: They demanded Moses stop speaking altogether.
options.note: They asked Moses to keep speaking to them, just not God directly; they did not want Moses silenced.

options.text: They showed no reaction at all.
options.note: Verse 18 explicitly records that they trembled and stood at a distance.

quiz.q: According to Moses in verse 20, why had God come in this terrifying way?

options.text: To test them, so that the fear of Him would keep them from sinning.
options.note: This is Moses' exact explanation of the purpose behind the terrifying display.

options.text: To punish them for a specific sin they had just committed.
options.note: No specific recent sin is cited; Moses frames it as a test meant to instill lasting reverence.

options.text: To frighten them into abandoning the covenant.
options.note: The purpose given is the opposite, to keep them faithful to the covenant through godly fear, not to drive them away.

options.text: No explanation is given for the terrifying display.
options.note: Verse 20 gives Moses' explicit explanation.

questions: God introduced Himself as redeemer before giving a single command. How well do you keep that same order, resting in what God has done before trying to obey what He asks?

The command against idols forbids not just false gods but any human attempt to shape God into something manageable. What image of God have you quietly built that is smaller or safer than who He actually is?
Israel was so overwhelmed by God's holiness that they begged for a mediator rather than face Him directly. How does knowing Christ is now your mediator change the way you approach God in prayer?
Jesus summarized all ten commands as love for God and love for neighbor. Which of the ten do you find easiest to reduce to a technical rule rather than living out as an act of love?

Moses said the fear of God was meant to keep the people from sinning, not to drive them away. Is your own reverence for God currently more likely to keep you close to Him or push you toward hiding from Him?

translationNotes.note: Visiting the iniquity of the fathers on their children reflects the observable reality of generational patterns of sin, not a claim that children are punished for guilt that is not their own; verse 6 balances it with far greater emphasis on loving devotion to a thousand generations.
Take the name of the LORD in vain covers more than casual cursing; it includes false oaths, hollow worship, and claiming God's authority for what He has not actually said or done.

Covet renders a Hebrew verb describing an inward desire that leads toward taking action, addressing the heart's longing rather than merely outward behavior, making this the only commandment explicitly aimed at internal desire.
